Cancer survival rates in the United States have improved significantly over the past three decades. According to the American Cancer Society's 2026 statistics report, the overall 5-year relative survival rate across all cancers combined has reached 70%, up from about 49% in the mid-1970s. Gains have been especially pronounced for historically fatal cancers — liver cancer survival rose from 7% to 22%, and lung cancer from 15% to 28%. However, several cancers remain extremely deadly, with survival rates that have seen only modest improvement.

1. Mesothelioma (~2,500–3,000 cases/year)
2. Adrenocortical carcinoma (~600 cases/year)
3. Small intestine cancer (~5,500 cases/year)
4. Gallbladder cancer (~4,800 cases/year)
5. Cholangiocarcinoma (~8,000 cases/year)

1. Mesothelioma [~12%]
2. Esophageal cancer [~22%]
3. Liver cancer [~22%]
4. Lung cancer [~28%]
5. Stomach cancer [~33%]
